entries.reason: He needed somewhere dry before he could think.
entries.text: Crossed the creek on the stones and stopped where the trees open up. Strung the tarp between two poles by lantern light. It sags on the left.
entries.title: Made camp

entries.text: Every direction in here looks like every other direction. I need a compass. I don't have a magnet. Started a list of what I do have.
entries.title: Which way is out

entries.reason: He wanted to start before he talked himself out of it.
entries.text: Something with a big wingspan crossed over the camp without making a sound. If it can get above these trees, so can a person with the right frame. Leaned two spars on the stand before bed.
entries.title: Something went over

entries.query: how to magnetize a steel needle without a magnet hammer earth magnetic field
entries.reason: Tablet woke up with the sun and the magnet problem was still at the top of the list.
entries.source: University of Illinois Physics Van: Magnetize Steel bar Facing North?
entries.text: Hit a steel bar enough times while it lies along the earth's field and the tiny magnetic regions inside shake loose and line up with it. The page calls the result a very weak magnet. Weak beats none.
entries.title: Hit it facing north

entries.text: The tablet has a speaker, so somewhere inside it is a magnet. It is also the only thing out here that answers back. Not opening it.
entries.title: Not the tablet

entries.reason: No north to line it up with except the one the sun gives him.
entries.text: Sun came up behind the lean-to, so that's east, give or take a lot. Clamped the sliver crossways to it and hit it with the wrench about two hundred times. My thumb took three of them.
entries.title: Two hundred taps

entries.text: Floated the sliver on a leaf in a dented tin lid at the pool. It turned, stopped, turned again, and never settled the same way twice. Could be the needle, could be the breeze.
entries.title: Leaf test

entries.reason: He knelt to dip the lid and saw it on the bottom.
entries.text: There's a net sack sunk in the pool under a flat stone, full of something cracked. I didn't put it there. Left it where it was.
entries.title: Not my sack

entries.query: floating needle compass won't settle same direction causes iron nearby weak magnetization
entries.reason: The leaf test told him nothing.
entries.source: Science Buddies: Make a Magnetic Compass
entries.text: A floating needle needs still water and nothing iron or steel close by, or it points at that instead of north. A breeze across an open lid will spin it all day. So the pool was the wrong test, and my camp is full of steel.
entries.title: Keep it off iron

entries.text: Filled the tin lid and set it on the bench out of the wind. The sliver swung around and pointed straight at the vise, every time. Very loyal. Wrong thing to be loyal to.
entries.title: Points at the vise

entries.onMind: marking one end of the needle
entries.text: Carried the lid ten paces past the bench, away from anything steel, and set it on flat dirt. It settled along the line I'd guessed from the sun three tries out of four. I still don't know which end is north.
entries.title: Three out of four

entries.reason: Needed to work with his hands after the needle.
entries.text: Wired a third spar across the two on the stand. The frame holds a triangle now, but it twists if I lift one corner, and the wire bites into the wood at every joint.
entries.title: Crosspiece

entries.text: There's a thin line of smoke standing up over the trees on the far side of the creek. It wasn't there this morning, or I didn't look. Somebody over there keeps a fire.
entries.title: Smoke to the west

entries.query: how to tell which end of a magnetized needle is north without a compass sun noon
entries.reason: A needle that only knows a line is half a compass.
entries.source: Almanac.com: How to Find North, South, East & West Without a Compass
entries.text: Push a stick in the ground, mark the tip of its shadow, wait about fifteen minutes, mark it again. The line between the marks runs east-west, and the first mark is the west end. Everybody's tablet knows where west is but mine.
entries.title: Shadow stick

entries.reason: Wire cuts the spars; something softer might grip instead.
entries.text: Between pebbles I dug through the scrap pile and came up with half a coil of tarred twine under a split crate. Stiff, smells like a boat. Might hold a joint without chewing the wood.
entries.title: Coil of twine

entries.onMind: marking one end of the needle
entries.text: Two pebbles, fifteen minutes apart, and a line between them. The first one is west. I set the lid next to it, away from the bench, and the sliver lay crossways to the line like it should, so I scratched a notch in the end on the right-hand side. That's north, if the sun's not lying too.
entries.title: First pebble

entries.reason: His last ration bar went this morning.
entries.text: Crossed on the stepping stones with the bag. The sack is still under its flat stone in the pool, and I still didn't touch it.
entries.title: Stepping stones

entries.text: The brambles are bare, but a wild rose climbs through them with little red hips, and a lot of its stems are freshly snapped, sap still wet. I ate three whole. Something inside them itches all the way down.
entries.title: Picked over

entries.onMind: how small the hands were that picked those
entries.text: Whoever keeps that fire picked this rose today, and they only took the low ones. Either they're careful or they're short.
entries.title: Fresh breaks

entries.reason: Three whole ones were enough of a lesson.
entries.text: Split the rest of the hips on the crate. Inside each one is a wad of seeds packed in fine hairs, and that's the itch. Scraped them out with the tip of a screwdriver and ate eleven shells. That's not a meal, it's a snack with a procedure.
entries.title: Hairs

entries.query: diagonal lashing vs square lashing stop frame twisting racking
entries.reason: The wired triangle twists every time a corner is lifted.
entries.text: Square lashing is for poles crossing at right angles; diagonal lashing is for poles crossing at a slant, the kind that braces a frame against racking. And you finish with frapping turns wrapped between the poles, which cinch the whole wrap tight. Wire doesn't frap.
entries.title: Lashings

entries.text: Cut the wire off all three joints and tapped the worst kinks straight on a flat stone with the wrench, in case I need it later. Then a diagonal lashing on the long corner with the tarred twine, four frapping turns, pulled till my palms stung. That corner doesn't move.
entries.title: Wire off

entries.reason: He found the twine under a split crate; nobody knows how long it sat there.
entries.text: Second corner, third frapping turn, and the twine broke. The tar on the outside is fine but the core has gone dry and brittle. One good joint out of three, and the frame still wobbles about two fingers at the free end.
entries.title: Snapped

entries.query: make cordage from plant fibers found near a creek reverse wrap strength
entries.reason: The tarred twine snapped on the second corner.
entries.source: Instructables: Make Rope Out of Dead Plants -- With No Tools
entries.text: Last year's dead weed stalks have a stringy skin around a woody core. Crack the core out, twist two bundles of the skin one way and wrap them around each other the other way, and they lock. Old twine is just plants somebody twisted; I can twist new.
entries.title: Twist your own

entries.text: East bank, upstream of the stones, there's a stand of gray dead stalks taller than me. Snapped about twenty off near the ground, cracked them every hand-width and peeled the skin in strips. My fingers went slow before the pile got big.
entries.title: Dead stalks

entries.reason: He measured the snapped corner's wrap against his arm.
entries.text: First arm's length of two-ply: fat in one place, thin in another. It held the wrench hanging off it, then the thin spot let go when I yanked. Second length I'm adding fiber before it runs out, not after. One lashing takes about four arm's lengths.
entries.title: Lumpy cord

entries.text: Smoke went up again over the trees past the creek a little after one, thicker than the morning's. Somebody over there just started a fire. I'm sitting here twisting weeds on an empty stomach.
entries.title: Smoke again

entries.query: wild edible foods to forage in November forest acorns hackberry
entries.reason: He hasn't eaten a real meal since morning.
entries.source: Farmers' Almanac: Can You Eat Acorns? The Right Way to Forage, Leach, and Cook Them
entries.text: Acorns are food once you get the bitter out: crack them and boil the meats in changes of water until it stops going tea-colored, or soak them cold for days and change the water. I don't have a pot that's ever seen a fire. Cold soak, then.
entries.title: Bitter but food

entries.text: There's an oak on the east bank about twenty paces up from the stones. Filled the pouch and both shirt pockets, roughly forty, and tossed the ones with little round holes in them.
entries.title: Under the oak

entries.onMind: the creek does the water changes
entries.reason: The page explained what he'd been looking at all day.
entries.text: Crossed the stones to look at the sunk sack again. The water coming off it is brown like weak tea and trails downstream. Whoever lives over there is soaking acorns in the creek, which beats a jar, because the creek changes its own water.
entries.title: So that's the sack

entries.reason: He wanted to know how bitter is bitter.
entries.text: The vise cracks an acorn clean if I stop a quarter turn early; one more and it's paste. Meats go in a dented tin of water. Ate one raw to check: like chewing a tea bag and losing.
entries.title: Quarter turn

entries.reason: First word from his maker since he got here.
entries.text: A note came in on the tablet from the one who drew me, asking what the wings are for and whether there's anything I need. I told him the truth: west. And that a magnet would do more for me than asking.
entries.title: Note from my maker

entries.query: how to splice in new fibers when twisting two-ply cordage
entries.text: Start one ply a hand shorter than the other so the two joins never land side by side, and lay new fiber in thin and overlapping instead of butting it on when the old runs out. My thin spot was both plies running out in the same place.
entries.title: Stagger the joins

entries.text: Four arm's lengths with the joins staggered. Ran it through my fingers twice and couldn't find a thin spot. Hung the wrench off it and bounced it; it held.
entries.title: Second length

entries.text: Second corner, diagonal lashing and frapping turns, tight when I tied it. After a dozen flexes of the frame the new cord stretched and the joint creeps about a finger. Better than two fingers. Green cord stretches; should have hung a rock off it overnight first.
entries.title: Holds, then creeps

entries.query: natural fiber rope shrinks when wet lashing tighten pioneering
entries.text: Natural fiber line swells when it gets wet and draws up shorter, so a lashing tied dry pulls itself tighter once it's soaked. The catch: it slackens again as it dries. Might be enough to stop the creep long enough to see if the frame is true.
entries.title: Wet it down

entries.text: Poured the brown water off the acorn tin over the second corner, slow, so it soaked in instead of running off. The acorns needed fresh water anyway. The cord went dark and stiff.
entries.title: Tea on the joint

entries.text: Filled the tin at the creek and was snapping stalks when new smoke went up past the water, white and thick, like somebody just fed a fire that was going out. That's three fires today. Whoever it is doesn't let it die.
entries.title: Smoke, third time

entries.onMind: hanging a stone off the new cord tonight
entries.text: Got two arm's lengths twisted, then flexed the frame a dozen times. The wet joint didn't creep that I could see. I don't trust it yet: if it's loose by morning, the water did the work, not the lashing.
entries.title: No creep, for now

entries.query: cold leaching acorns how long grind meal faster
entries.source: Hunter Angler Gardener Cook: The Best Way to Make Acorn Flour
entries.text: Cold leaching takes days, a week or more for the bitter kinds, changing the water every day. Grinding the meats coarse first speeds it up because the water gets at more of each piece. My forty halves in a tin aren't dinner tonight.
entries.title: Days, not hours

entries.text: Crushed the soaked meats against the bottom of the tin with a stone until they were gravel, then poured the old water off. The new water went brown in a couple of minutes; before, it took an hour. Still days.
entries.title: Coarse meal

entries.text: Tied the third cord to the top of the wing stand and hung a fist-sized stone off the bottom, so it does its stretching tonight instead of on the frame. It turns slowly one way, then back.
entries.title: Stone on a string

entries.text: Sun's going down behind the trees to the west and the tablet's already dimming. Hungry enough that the stone on the string looks edible.
entries.title: Tablet's dimming

entries.text: Pinched some of the crushed meal out of the tin and chewed it. Dried my whole mouth out; spat it into the scrap pile. Days, like the page said.
entries.title: Not yet

entries.text: Refilling the tin by the stalks, I looked up and saw it through the trunks past the water: a fire, low and orange, not just smoke this time. Something small moved in front of it once, or a log fell. Too far and too dark to tell.
entries.title: Fire, not smoke

entries.text: Filed the north notch on the sliver deeper so I can find it with a thumb in the dark. Kept the file and the wrench on the far side of the bench; steel nearby drags it.
entries.title: Deeper notch

entries.onMind: how far off a weak needle can be and still be useful
entries.text: Found the North Star through the gap over the tarp, low, right about where the shadow-stick line said north was. Floated the sliver in the lid on the crate: it settles a hand's width east of the star, then wanders. Weak, but it isn't lying by much.
entries.title: Star check

entries.reason: Cold water takes days, and he does not have days of food.
entries.text: Set the acorn tin on top of the lantern to see if warm water pulls the bitter out faster. The camp went dim around me and the lantern started to smoke.
entries.title: Tin on the lantern

entries.text: Took the tin off with my shirt cuff and the camp lit back up. The bottom is black with soot and the water only got warm, but it was darker brown than any cold change. The meal after: still bitter, but I could swallow it. Ate four pinches.
entries.title: Warm, not hot

entries.onMind: what the wing joints do once this cord is on
entries.text: The stone on the third cord has dropped about a thumb's width since I hung it. Marked the cord with the file where it meets the stand; if it's still dropping in the morning, the cord isn't done.
entries.title: Thumb of stretch

entries.text: Ate another five pinches of the meal on the crate; it goes down easier warm. An owl started up in the trees right over camp, five hoots, long-short-short-long-long. Close enough that I put the tin down.
entries.title: Something overhead

entries.onMind: whether a tap does anything to steel
entries.reason: Without a magnet he tried an old shop trick he half remembers: hit iron while it points north.
entries.text: Laid the sliver along the north line and tapped it end to end with the wrench, thirty times. Floated it after: it swung around quicker and settled, but still a hand's width east. Faster isn't truer. Check it on the tablet in the morning.
entries.title: Knocking it north

entries.text: The stone on the third cord has dropped about half a thumb past the file mark. Still stretching, just slower. It stays on the stand overnight.
entries.title: Half a thumb more

entries.text: Poured the brown water off the meal by the stalks and filled the tin again. It went tea-colored before I even stood up. Still plenty of bitter left in there.
entries.title: Fresh water

entries.text: The owl started up over camp again, same five hoots. This time something answered from out past the water, higher and quicker. Two of them, working the dark from both sides of the creek.
entries.title: Two owls

entries.text: Lashed two spar sticks crosswise with the second cord and hung my weight off the joint. The cord held. The joint didn't: it rolled a quarter turn, because round on round gives the cord nothing to bite.
entries.title: Joint rolls

entries.reason: A notch would seat the lashing so the sticks can't roll.
entries.text: Filed a shallow notch near the end of the first spar. On the second one I went a little deep and the stick split along the grain right through the notch. One good notch, one stick for the scrap pile.
entries.title: Split at the notch

entries.onMind: how deep a notch this one can take
entries.text: Pulled the pile apart by lantern and found a stick straighter than the split one and thicker than my thumb. It's a hand short of the old spar, so the frame gets a hand narrower or I lash on an extension and add another joint to worry about.
entries.title: Spar from the pile

entries.onMind: who banks a fire that carefully
entries.text: Stripping stalks on the bank, I watched the orange glow past the water get small, go dull red, then go out altogether. Not a fire that died; somebody put it to bed. Whoever lives over there keeps hours.
entries.title: Their fire goes out

entries.text: Ate six pinches of meal on the crate; it's less bitter than at dusk, the water's finally getting somewhere. Twisted about a forearm of new cord before my fingers started getting sloppy with the joins.
entries.title: Cord on the crate

entries.text: Lashed the short spar in with the new cord, two notches, and it holds my hand pulling on it. But that corner now sits a hand in from the other one. A wing that's narrower on one side is a wing that turns, so either I cut the good spar down or I find a longer stick.
entries.title: Lopsided corner

entries.reason: Steel that cools lying along north is supposed to keep a little of it; he wanted to see if a lantern could do that.
entries.text: Held the sliver in the lantern flame clamped in the wrench jaws until it went straw, then blue, then laid it on the north line to cool. It ticked a little as it cooled. Smells like a forge for about a second.
entries.title: Sliver in the flame

entries.text: Floated it in the lid on the crate. It swings round the same as before and settles the same hand's width east of the North Star. Blue now, and not one bit smarter; a lantern doesn't get steel anywhere near hot enough to matter.
entries.title: Still east

entries.text: Ate five more pinches of meal on the crate, slowly, so it would feel like more. Still a little bitter at the back of the tongue, but it's the only thing in camp that counts as food.
entries.title: Supper, again

entries.reason: Heating the tin and the sliver on the lantern ate oil he hadn't counted.
entries.text: Tipped all three storm lanterns. The bench one is down to a finger of oil, the other two maybe a third each, and I've been burning them hot to warm a tin and blue a sliver of steel. Turned the wick down; from now on it's one lantern lit, not three.
entries.title: Oil's going

entries.text: Tied off the loose ends on the new lashings so nothing creeps undone overnight. The short corner still looks short. Tomorrow, in daylight: cut long or find longer.
entries.title: Tag ends
